full_article:
Story by Pratik Ghimire Published on Sep 14, 2026

Before the streets of Nepal’s Bramhakhel fill with traffic, 40-year-old Pratima Poudel walks to a centuries-old stone spout carrying empty plastic bottles to collect water. The walk has become part of the Nepali language instructor’s daily routine.

The spout she visits each morning is part of the Kathmandu Valley’s traditional water system, composed of interconnected stone spouts known locally as dhunge dhara or alternately as hiti. The network once supplied water to communities across the valley; today, it provides an alternative source for residents facing unreliable access to piped water.

“We don’t like tap water,” she tells Next City as she fills her bottles directly from the spout. From time to time, residents treat the spout’s water with chlorine. “This water is cleaner. Some neighbors have begun boiling the water before drinking, but I am not worried.”

In a country where only a quarter of the population has access to clean drinking water, Poudel is one of a growing number of Kathmandu residents choosing the spout over the tap. Nearly 70% of the city’s drinking water samples contain E. coli and faecal coliform, bacteria that indicate contamination by human or animal waste, according to the latest government analysis. Residents say the valley’s rivers have become open sewers and the pipes carry the same contamination into their homes.

Climate change and rapid urbanization are colliding in the Southeast Asian country, where increased monsoon intensity and frequent floods are overwhelming the capital’s water systems. Amid this failure of modern infrastructure, residents are reviving dhunge dharas in and around Kathmandu — in one case, even rebuilding an ancient fountain from the ground up after it was lost in the 2015 earthquake.

Pratima Poudel fills her water bottle at Brahmakhel Dhunge Dhara in Kathmandu, Nepal. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

A 1,400-year-old network

The oldest functioning spout — Manga Hiti in Patan, a city of ancient palaces and courtyards less than four miles south of central Kathmandu — has provided water since 570 AD.

These fountains rely on underground aquifers that channel water naturally through gravitational force, supported by networks of ponds and canals that store and regulate supply during dry seasons while preventing flooding during monsoons.

Beneath each stone spout lies a complex water system. A stone spout is essentially “the outlet of a spring connected to groundwater,” as climate change and springshed expert Ujjwal Upadhyay describes it.

“The stone structure is built by people, but the water flowing through it comes from a natural underground system,” he explains.

Rainwater enters the ground through a defined recharge area, accumulates in underground aquifers and eventually emerges at the surface as a spring. Traditionally, communities identified these natural water pathways and built spouts at points where water could flow to the surface.

“Even those who get tap water come to Bhinya Hiti for drinking water,” says heritage conservationist Rabindra Puri, referring to a spout in Bhaktapur municipality, about eight miles from Kathmandu. It’s believed to date back around 1,400 years.

“The spouts served a social purpose as well as providing water,” he explains. “They were designed as community spaces where residents could meet, exchange news, and socialize while collecting water, much like people gathering at tea shops today.”

The Bhinya Hiti fountain in Bhaktapur, an ancient city in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire

Short supply, uncertain quality

The public utility company Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited is responsible for the management of the Kathmandu Valley’s water supply and sanitation system. Its 2024-2025 annual report says the capital’s water demand is about 136 million gallons (514 million liters) per day, while the company’s average supply is only 61.4 million (232.4 million liters) daily with seasonal variation.

The gap between supply and demand has pushed people to alternatives like groundwater extraction, private tankers, jars, and bottled water. But in places where functioning stone spouts are available, people continue to use dhunge dharas.

For 18-year-old Mohin Thapa, Brahmakhel Dhunge Dhara has made collecting drinking water easier.

“When my parents are busy with work, I collect the water myself,” the university student says. “Rather than going every day, I fill four or five bottles at a time, which lasts a couple of days.”

His family uses tap water for bathing, cleaning, gardening and washing, while relying on water from the stone spout for drinking.

“I prefer drinking water from the dhunge dhara,” he tells Next City . “Ever since I was a child, that has been my primary water source, and I love its natural taste and freshness.”

Children drink water from Alko Hiti in the city of Patan. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

Sher Bahadur Pun, chief of the Tropical and Infectious Disease Hospital’s Clinical Research Unit, says the hospital receives around half a dozen patients presenting with symptoms of waterborne diseases, including fever and diarrhea, every day. Patients do not typically identify stone-spout water as the source of their illness, he says, but he still encourages caution.

“That does not make untreated stone-spout water automatically safe,” Pun says. “Boiling or purifying would be better.”

A 2022 review of research on Kathmandu Valley’s stone spouts reported that previous testing had detected total coliforms, E. coli and nitrates in some spout-water samples, with water quality varying by season. The review noted that many stone spouts rely on shallow groundwater, making them vulnerable to contamination.

A system under pressure

A survey by the Kathmandu Valley Water Supply Management Board in 2019 counted 573 spouts in the valley with a combined discharge of 2.4 million liters a day.

Of those spouts, many were in disrepair and 94 had been lost entirely. Just 224 were still functioning. In 2022, the valley’s water fountains were placed on the the World Monuments Fund’s watchlist for heritage sites urgently at risk.

Like the city’s modern water infrastructure, the ancient water network has also been increasingly under pressure due to extreme weather and development. Kathmandu receives around 57 inches (1,450 millimetres) of rainfall a year, but more often, that rain is falling in shorter, more intense periods, Upadhyay says.

“Heavy rainfall over a short duration is more likely to run off rather than infiltrate and recharge groundwater,” Upadhyay points out.

Houses, roads, agriculture and other changes in land use can interfere with the areas where water needs to infiltrate, he explains: “A spout can be cleaned, repaired or restored on the surface, but if its underground conduits are broken, its recharge area is blocked, or its water source has been disrupted, the flow can disappear.”

Sushil Shrestha stands beside Alko Hiti in the city of Patan, Nepal. (Photo by Pratik Ghimire)

Sushil Shrestha, a stone-spout expert, conservationist and chairperson of the Historic Stone Spouts and Ponds Conservation Association, says that this has happened at stone spouts across the valley.

He points to Sundhara, or the Golden Spout, in Kathmandu, where surrounding buildings and infrastructure have disrupted the underground system and contributed to the spout drying up. But he says the spout could still be revived by reconnecting it to viable water sources.

Bringing spouts back to life

Residents are now more aware of the importance of this heritage, Shrestha says.

The nearly 600- to 700-year-old Alko Hiti in Patan, Lalitpur — which alone produces more than 200,000 gallons (about 800,000 liters) of water a day, he says — was restored after its water was polluted from a leak from a local bone mill factory in 2000. A surge in water-borne diseases triggered a local conservation movement, which culminated in the community-led revival and renovation of Alko Hiti in 2003.

In Thamel, the historic Ga Hiti spout supplied thousands of residents until April 2015, when a neighbouring hotel collapsed in a massive earthquake that devastated the region, and the spout was destroyed. Reconstruction cost more than $30,000 (Rs4.6 million), with Kathmandu Metropolitan City covering 80% and residents raising the rest. The Ga Hiti Youth Club and local volunteers finished the work in about six months, and the spout was flowing again by early 2017.

According to Shrestha, there is a massive gap between water demand and supply, and functioning dhunge dhara are “actively helping to minimize that gap.”

“They are priceless ancient heritage and very old living historic monuments – beyond easing daily shortages,” he tells Next City . “If Kathmandu Valley loses them or they stop flowing, the water crisis will deepen further, and we will lose a very important part of our history.”

title: Floods damage 1,843 tons of vegetables in Nepal - FreshPlaza
description: Floods damage 1,843 tons of vegetables in Nepal  FreshPlaza
publisher.title: FreshPlaza
full_article:
Flash floods that affected the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system on August 26 caused losses to vegetable cultivation across several areas of Nepal, according to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment report prepared by the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The assessment found that 137 hectares of vegetable crops were affected, resulting in an estimated loss of 1,843 tons of vegetables.

Bidur in Nuwakot recorded the largest impact, with 98 hectares of vegetable crops affected and an estimated potential loss of 1,323 tons.

Vegetable growing areas were also affected in Dhading. This included nine hectares in Benighat Rorang, seven hectares in Gajuri, two hectares in Siddhalek, and 14 hectares in Galchhi.

The assessment identified affected local levels across Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, including Bidur, Likhu, Belkotgadhi, Benighat Rorang, Gajuri, Siddhalek, Galchhi, Gandaki, and Shahid Lakhan.

title: New York Book Sale Raises Over $1,500 for Nepal Flood Victims - nepyork
description: New York Book Sale Raises Over $1,500 for Nepal Flood Victims  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — A community book sale and literary gathering in Jackson Heights raised $1,502 for families affected by flooding in Nepal, bringing authors, readers, journalists and community members together around books, conversation and disaster relief.

The event, “Books for Flood Victims — Stories That Give Hope,” was held Sept. 13 at Himalayan Yak Restaurant in Jackson Heights. More than 70 people attended, according to organizers.

The money was raised through book sales. Organizers clarified after the event that no cash donations of any kind were accepted and that the entire $1,502 was generated through the sale of books donated by participating authors and literary figures. The $1,502, equivalent to about 230,000 Nepali rupees, will be used to support families affected by the floods, organizers said. The full amount will be deposited into the Nepal government’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, according to the organizers. They said details of the deposit and transfer will be made public to ensure transparency.

Participants browse books donated by Nepali and Nepal-connected authors. Photo: NepYork

The event was organized by authors Passang Nuru Sherpa and Pratikshya Thakali, in association with Khasokhas, NepYork and the AINAS New York Chapter, which served as co-organizers. Thakali also moderated the evening.

Authors and literary figures from Nepal and the international community participated in the gathering, selling their books in person and speaking with readers. Writers, journalists, representatives of community organizations, social workers and literature enthusiasts were among those attending.

Participants purchased books as a way of expressing solidarity with families affected by the floods, turning the act of buying literature into a form of humanitarian support.

A Community Organizer’s Pandemic Memoir

Passang Nuru Sherpa, one of the event’s organizers, is a Nepali-American author, lyricist and entrepreneur based in Jackson Heights. His experience during the COVID-19 pandemic later became the basis for Behind the Mask: A Pandemic Memoir . Originally written in Nepali under the title Corona Katha , the book was translated into English by Mahesh Paudyal and journalist Peter Gill.

The 449-page memoir chronicles Sherpa’s experience in Jackson Heights during the pandemic, when Queens was among the early epicenters of the outbreak in the United States. Based on diary entries and personal observations, the book follows Sherpa’s transformation from salon owner to community responder.

Through the Coronavirus Awareness and Support Group, he helped deliver food, medicine and other essential supplies to families confined to their homes.

Passang Nuru Sherpa, one of the organizers of the “Books for Flood Victims — Stories That Give Hope” fundraiser, stands with his book, Behind the Mask: A Pandemic Memoir, in Jackson Heights, New York. Photo: NepYork

Behind the Mask was among the books available at the fundraiser. Peter Gill spoke about his experience translating the memoir and about the book’s portrayal of the pandemic, Jackson Heights and the resilience of immigrant communities.

The book is divided into sections covering life before the pandemic, lockdown, grassroots relief efforts and the period after restrictions eased. It combines Sherpa’s personal reflections with accounts of his neighbors’ struggles, Nepali cultural traditions and the ways immigrant communities responded to the crisis.

A Story Rooted in Thini

Renée Thakali and Pratikshya Thakali, co-authors of The Joyous Fort, Our Homeland in Thini, also participated in the event and spoke about their book and their connection to Thini, a historic Thakali village in Nepal’s Mustang District.

Renée Thakali first traveled to Nepal in 1977 as a Peace Corps volunteer. What began as an assignment developed into a lifelong connection to Nepal, including her relationship with the people and community of Thini, where she met her future husband and his family.

Renée Thakali and Pratikshya Thakali pose during the “Books for Flood Victims — Stories That Give Hope” fundraiser in Jackson Heights, New York, on Sept. 13. Photo: NepYork

She later spent more than 37 years working as a forester for the U.S. Forest Service and Peace Corps Nepal. Her international forestry assignments also took her to Afghanistan, the Philippines and Saipan, where she worked on forest restoration and trained local forestry workers.

Pratikshya Thakali was born and raised in Nepal and spent her early years in Thini. Growing up in the close-knit community gave her an understanding of Thakali traditions, language and values.

Books by Pratikshya Thakali and Renée Thakali are displayed on a table. Photo: NepYork

She was particularly influenced by stories from her grandfather about trade journeys across India and Tibet. She later immigrated to the United States amid Nepal’s political turmoil and earned a bachelor’s degree in business administration from Baruch College, City University of New York.

During the program, Renée Thakali also shared her observations about the changing conditions in the Himalayan region and the effects of global warming, drawing on her experiences and connection to Nepal.

A Mountaineer’s Warning About Climate Change

Another featured author was Lakpa Dendi Sherpa, a world-record-holding mountaineer, high-altitude guide and author of Himalayan Maverick.

Copies of the autobiography were available at the fundraiser, with Sherpa saying that proceeds from books sold that evening would go toward disaster relief. He did not speak at the event, but his book was presented as part of the literary and humanitarian effort.

Sherpa’s book and life story also brought a climate-change perspective to the gathering. His experiences in the Himalayas and the Arctic have shaped his observations about the changing environment.

Dr. Rajan Thapaliya holds a copy of Himalayan Maverick by Lakpa Dendi Sherpa, a world-record-holding mountaineer, high-altitude guide and author. Photo: NepYork

“Years ago, the melting of the Khumbu Glacier on Everest usually began around the end of May. Today, I see it starting weeks earlier, around the middle of May,” he said in remarks prepared for the event.

“For a mountaineer, climate change is not just something we read about. We see it, we walk on it, and we experience it.”

Sherpa has reached the summit of Mount Everest 11 times and completed more than 30 ascents of 8,000-meter peaks, including K2, Lhotse and Manaslu.

In 2018, he set a Guinness World Record for the fastest triple ascent of Mount Everest in a single season, reaching the summit three times in 10 days, 18 hours and 30 minutes. He has also been involved in major Himalayan expeditions, including Nimsdai Purja’s Project Possible 14 Peaks challenge.

He currently serves as a director of Taktok Brothers Treks & Expedition, where he leads technical rope-fixing teams, high-altitude rescues and commercial expeditions in the Himalayas.

Sherpa has said that his experiences in the mountains and the Arctic have shown him that climate change is already reshaping the natural environment.

“The Himalayas and the Arctic may be far apart, but they are connected,” he said. “The Himalayas, known as the ‘Third Pole,’ provide freshwater to millions of people.”

As glaciers retreat, he said, the risks of floods and landslides increase for communities in Nepal.

“Nature has no borders, so we must work together to protect our planet,” Sherpa said.

Lakpa Dendi Sherpa browses a book by journalist Kishor Panthi. Photo: NepYork

He ended his message with a call to pay attention to both scientific evidence and the observations of people who live and work in vulnerable environments.

“From the highest mountain on Earth to the Arctic Ocean, the message is clear: Let us listen to the mountains. Let us listen to the Arctic. And most importantly, let us listen to science,” he said. “Protecting our planet means protecting our future.”

Speakers From the Nepali Community

The program also included remarks from Januka Osti Dhakal, Kishor Panthi, Kishan Singh Dhami, Padma Linkha Magar, Laxmi Shrestha and Tsomo Dasel, among others. Literary figures including Kishan Dhami, Laxmi Shrestha and Padma Linkha Magar added a literary dimension to the program through poetry readings.

Dasel, the owner of Himalayan Yak, expressed gratitude to the organizers, authors and community members for coming together to support a humanitarian cause through literature and community engagement. Rajkumar Bista, president of the Himalayan Buddhist Community, also offered remarks and wished the organizers success with the humanitarian initiative.

Authors, organizers, speakers and participants pose for a group photo after the “Books for Flood Victims — Stories That Give Hope” fundraiser in Jackson Heights, New York, on Sept. 13.

Januka Osti Dhakal, president of the AINAS New York Chapter, delivered a vote of thanks on behalf of the co-organizing organization.

Their participation brought together perspectives from the Nepali diaspora, journalism, literature, community life and local business in New York.

The event was intentionally structured differently from a conventional literary gathering. Organizers kept formalities and lengthy speeches to a minimum, emphasizing direct interaction between authors and readers, introductions to books and the humanitarian purpose of the fundraiser.

Organizers said the format was designed to place direct interaction among authors, readers and community members at the center of the event rather than lengthy formalities and speeches.

Children’s books are displayed on a table. Photo: NepYork

Rather than simply presenting books, the gathering sought to turn their sale into a form of community support for people affected by the disaster in Nepal.

“The main objective was not only to sell books, but to use literature and creativity as a means of humanitarian service,” said Passang Nuru Sherpa, one of the organizers.

The organizers said the broader goal was to express the Nepali diaspora’s support, goodwill and solidarity with families affected by the disaster while demonstrating how literature and creative work can contribute to humanitarian service.

A Khasokhas magazine, three books by Khasokhas Editor-in-Chief Kishor Panthi, “Khasokhas: Local Journalism Matters” stickers and materials promoting Khasokhas’s initiative to encourage direct donations to Nepal’s government disaster relief fund are displayed on a table. Photo: NepYork

The event also gave members of the Nepali diaspora an opportunity to express solidarity with families affected by the floods.

Authors and community members had been invited to donate books or purchase works by participating writers. The books donated by the authors formed the basis of the fundraising effort, with the organizers saying that the proceeds from their sale would be directed entirely to disaster relief. Books in both Nepali and English were available, with authors present to introduce their work and speak with readers.

A Broad Collection of Nepali and Nepal-Connected Books

The fundraiser featured a wide-ranging collection of books by Nepali and Nepal-connected writers, with authors and their works represented throughout the evening.

In addition to the authors profiled above, the collection included books by Lakpa Gurung, Pema Sherpa, Sushila Shrestha, Jyoti Paudyal, Sharda Chhetri, Gita Chhetri, Poonam Kaphle, Bishnu Niraula, Dr. Abhi Subedi, Salil Gyawali, Kiran Dhungana and Radheshyam Lekali.

Sita Kharel shows a book about Sahana Pradhan by author Sushila Shrestha.

Other featured authors included Dr. Hiranya Gyawali, Shree Om Shrestha, Anand Shrestha, Maheshwar Panta, Govinda Giri “Prerana,” Sundar Pratap Rana, Babita Basnet, Krishna Gautam and Dr. Shashi Thapa Pandit.

The collection also included works by Arjun Prasad Mainali, Dr. Bishwabandhu Sharma and Dirgha Raj Upadhyay. Mahila Suraksha Dababa Samuha was represented as a publishing organization.

Books by Kishan Singh Dhami, Laxmi Shrestha, Kishor Panthi and Januka Osti Dhakal were also among those available at the event, alongside works by the authors featured in the program.

The breadth of the collection reflected the event’s broader effort to connect literature, community and humanitarian support, while giving readers an opportunity to discover works representing Nepali experiences in Nepal and the diaspora.

Books in Nepali and English were offered for sale. Photo: NepYork

Organizers said the response to the format was positive and that similar events could be held in the future to support other causes.

They said the event’s unconventional format was positively received by participants, who appreciated the emphasis on literature, direct community interaction and humanitarian service.

They thanked the authors and literary figures who made books available, readers who purchased them, guests, community organizations, journalists, volunteers and others who helped organize and support the fundraiser.

The organizers specifically expressed gratitude to the authors and literary figures who donated their books, readers who purchased them, guests, community organizations, journalists and media workers, volunteers and others who supported the campaign directly or indirectly.

Authors speak with and interact with participants.

For the organizers, the more than 70 people who attended and the $1,502 raised represented only part of the event’s success. They said the positive response to the unconventional format — and the effort to connect literature, community and humanitarian service — was equally important.

title: A Flood Disaster in Nepal - Foreign Policy in Focus
description: A Flood Disaster in Nepal  Foreign Policy in Focus
publisher.title: Foreign Policy in Focus
full_article:
The flash floods that swept through Nepal on August 26 came from a glacial crash, 40 miles from Kathmandu, the country’s capital. A gigantic chunk of ice, half a kilometer thick, broke off a glacier and fell down a river with a seismic force of 5.2 magnitude. This mass of millions of tons of ice shattered on impact into a gushing stream that increased the level of the Bhote Koshi River, which sits at the intersection of the Sino-Nepali border, by nine meters. The Bhote Koshi River merges with the larger river system of Trishuli that, too, got bloated and pushed floodwater almost a hundred miles downstream across Nepal’s border into India.

As of September 5, as many as 1,350 people were listed dead and 5,000 missing. Initial estimates put the economic toll of the disaster at $5 billion, which is 10 percent of Nepal’s GDP. Kathmandu calls the disaster anything but natural and demands “justice and compensation” from “the world’s major emitters.”

Nepal is home to 3,808 Himalayan glaciers spanning 3,902 square kilometers with an ice cover of 286.1 billion cubic meters of water. These glaciers are, however, retreating fast. The reason behind their retreat is rapidly changing global climate. It is not just Nepal’s glaciers that are melting away. Nepal is part of the eight nations that share 54,000 Hindu Kush-Himalayas glaciers, which hold 5.6 trillion cubic meters of water. These glaciers, which are billed as the “water towers of Asia,” feed Asia’s 10 largest river systems. They are also known as the world’s “third pole,” the other two being the North and South Poles.

Although estimates vary, one-third of these glaciers will have melted away by the turn of the century, if global heating reaches 1.5 degree Celsius above preindustrial levels. This will be an irreparable loss for 2 billion people of the region, who depend upon them for drinking and irrigation supplies. A case in point is the Indus, which is one of the largest river systems in south Asia which depends on glaciers for 80 percent of its annual flow. The rapid melting of these glaciers, triggered by global heating, is the death knell for the region’s ecology, as well as its agriculture and agriculture-related industries.

Glaciers are fed by precipitation, especially the monsoons. As climate change has shortened the monsoon season, precipitation across the Hindu Kush-Himalayas has dropped in direct proportion. Worse still, global heating is thinning out the existing ice cover of the glaciers. Nepali glaciers have lost one-third of their ice cover. More importantly, the Himalayas are reportedly “warming twice as fast as the global average.” Although the glaciers at the top remain somewhat replenished by precipitation, climate change is stripping them bare at lower elevation.

The giant ice chunk that snapped off a glacier on August 26 was also at the lower elevation, where snowpack was too weak to hold it in place. In 2011-2020, the region’s glaciers melted 65 percent faster than the decade before. Climate change is, thus, hollowing out these glaciers in three ways. Lack of precipitation leaves them with ever-diminishing ice cover. Global heating is fast melting their preexisting ice cover. And the declining snow and ice cover, which is reflecting less and less sunlight, absorbs more and more heat, accelerating glacial melting in the process.

The site of the Nepali glacier that cracked up on August 26 was the Langtang Lirung peak close to the Langtang National Park, which borders Tibet in China. Around a hundred miles downstream, India also endured loss of life in the glacial collapse. As such it is a cross-national calamity. What gives it a global cast is the suspected loss of life of thousands of tourists from 34 countries, including 75 from the United States. These nations represent four continents of Africa, Americas, Asia, and Europe.

This is a snapshot of the global reach of fossil-fueled disasters that are increasing both in frequency and intensity by the year. Fossil fuels dug in Australia or burned in the United States have real life consequences half-way around the globe, to which even thousands of their own citizens are not immune. The global tale of woes, however, does not end here. On the Chinese side of the border, hundreds of tourists are unaccounted. Two weeks after the disaster, 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are still missing in China. Although the Nepali government is trying hard to account for every tourist, hopes for their survival are dimming by the day.

The destructive force of the flooding can be gauged at the Sino-Nepali border crossing. Both sides of the border are crisscrossed with shiny customs and immigration buildings that, until before the disaster struck, stood tall. What happened to these buildings when the nine-meter high walls of water crashed into them is a harrowing sight to watch. It took only a second or two to rip them from their foundations and toss them like toys into torrents of water. The same held true for untold numbers of hapless staff and aspirant migrants who tried to sprint away only to be swallowed up by the tide in the blink of an eye.

The World Meteorological Organization confirms that the 11 years since 2015 were the hottest on record. Global temperatures have already reached 1.4 degree Celsius and are projected to reach 1.8 degree Celsius by midcentury, way over the maximum threshold of 1.5 degree Celsius agreed in the Paris Climate Pact.

Some attribute the recent accelerated warming to the El Nino effect, implying that all this global heating is transitory and fueled by a natural phenomenon. That’s not true. Even El Nino has grown 37 percent more intense due to global warming. El Nino is the result of warmer than normal waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, a warming that is driven by climate change. Also, warming Pacific waters are supercharging El Nino. El Nino, in turn, is exacerbating the impact of climate change, making glacial collapses more frequent and even more fatal.

The flood disaster in Nepal is a canary in a coal mine. It should alert the world to the dangers of the continued use of fossil fuels and of not zeroing out emissions. The planet is warming, the glaciers are changing, and disasters just keep happening.

title: NYC Restaurant Himalayan Yak Donates $5,000 from Buffet Sales to Nepal Flood Relief - nepyork
description: NYC Restaurant Himalayan Yak Donates $5,000 from Buffet Sales to Nepal Flood Relief  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
JACKSON HEIGHTS, N.Y. — Himalayan Yak Restaurant has donated $5,000 to the Government of Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support flood relief efforts in Nepal after partnering with Nepal Run USA to raise money through buffet sales in Jackson Heights, organizers said.

The restaurant, located at 72-20 Roosevelt Ave., raised $4,070 through buffet purchases made by runners, customers and other community members. Himalayan Yak covered all food and preparation costs, allowing the full amount collected through buffet sales to go toward relief efforts.

The restaurant contributed an additional $930 from its own funds, bringing the total donation to $5,000.

Tsomo Dasel, owner of Himalayan Yak, said the contribution was intended to show solidarity with people affected by the flooding in Nepal.

title: Nepal adopts resolution on cooperation in nature conservation in Asia - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal adopts resolution on cooperation in nature conservation in Asia  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Kathmandu, Nepal, participants in the 6th Asian Congress for Conservation Biology adopted the Kathmandu Resolution 2026. It calls for stronger regional cooperation, leadership development and support for local and Indigenous communities in conserving biodiversity. This was stated in a commentary published by Mongabay.

The congress took place in early June under the theme “Harmonizing Biodiversity and Human Well-being in Asia.” It was organized by the Asian regional section of the Society for Conservation Biology together with the organization’s Nepal chapter and the Burhan Community Regeneration and Conservation Foundation.

Participants and program

Nearly 500 conservationists from 42 countries took part in the event. According to data cited in the commentary, 390 participants represented countries of the Global South, 357 were early-career professionals, and 151 were students. Another 38 people identified themselves as representatives of Indigenous or local communities, while 43% identified as women or members of gender minorities.

The program included 11 plenary speeches, 300 oral presentations across 24 sessions and 19 symposia, 59 poster presentations, as well as five afternoon and seven full-day workshops. Participants discussed the conservation of the Asiatic cheetah, Arabian and snow leopards, elephants, primates, birds, amphibians and reptiles, as well as human-wildlife interactions, the role of communities and conservation policy.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Content of the resolution

The Kathmandu Resolution calls for building the capacity of Asia’s conservation sector through peaceful regional interaction, the exchange of knowledge and experience, resource mobilization, and strengthening national chapters of the Society for Conservation Biology. The document also addresses the need to counter economic systems that view nature solely as capital for exploitation.

The resolution stresses the need to create conditions for leadership by students, women, gender minorities, Indigenous peoples and local communities. It calls for abandoning top-down conservation approaches in favor of models that recognize community rights, their independent decision-making, and the connection between nature conservation and public well-being.

The organizers provided nearly 160 participants with travel cost reimbursements, registration fee waivers or discounts. At the same time, some students said that the $229 fee for representatives of low- and middle-income countries who are members of the Society for Conservation Biology was too high.

title: US Adds $1 Million to Nepal Flood Response, Sends Forensic Experts - indiawest.com
description: US Adds $1 Million to Nepal Flood Response, Sends Forensic Experts  indiawest.com
publisher.title: indiawest.com
full_article:
US Adds $1 Million To Nepal Flood Response, Deploys Forensic Experts

WASHINGTON, DC- The United States has approved an additional $1 million to help Nepal identify victims of devastating floods, bringing State Department assistance for the disaster response to more than $5 million as American forensic specialists work alongside Nepal Police.

The new funding will provide forensic support to Nepal Police, the State Department said in a September 12 media note. The money was approved by the department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs as part of efforts to support the Nepali government in identifying victims.

US officials are working with Nepal Police to determine the most urgent requirements, including DNA analysis kits. The forensic assistance adds to US funding for emergency food, shelter, healthcare and other relief for flood-affected communities.

FBI forensic specialists are also working alongside Nepal Police on disaster victim identification. Their work is intended to help authorities identify those who died and provide answers to families of American citizens and other victims, the State Department said.

The largest component of the State Department’s assistance is $3 million for food and logistics through its global assistance award with the World Food Program.

A further $365,000 is supporting health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene assistance through Jhpiego, FHI 360 and UNICEF. Together with the newly approved forensic funding, the listed State Department allocations total $5.05 million.

The US military has separately delivered 5,000 specialized disaster victim recovery supplies, 500 first aid kits, stretchers and front-end loaders. The equipment is supporting Nepal-led search, rescue and recovery operations.

A four-person US Military Civil Affairs Team is also on the ground to help address humanitarian needs following the disaster.

“The safety of Americans in the affected area remains our highest priority,” the State Department said, expressing sympathy for those affected and their families and reaffirming US friendship with the Nepali people.

“As the Secretary has reiterated, the United States is prepared to work closely with the Government of Nepal to continue to deliver additional assistance that responds directly to Nepal’s needs,” the department said. (IANS)

title: India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects - Al Jazeera
description: India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
India has approved the expedited export of electricity to neighbouring Nepal to help it overcome shortages caused by extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure from devastating floods last month.

In a statement on Monday, India’s Ministry of Power said up to 654 megawatts of electricity would be transmitted for 18 hours per day until December 31.

“The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal,” it said.

It added that in December it would also review the amount of power to be exported from January.

The flooding, triggered on August 26 by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.

At least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal were hit, with at least 900 power station workers among the more than 5,500 people still missing in the country.

Almost 100 percent of the country’s energy needs were met by hydropower before the floods hit. Since then, Nepal has been forced to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.

People cross a river via a zip line in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on September 11, 2026 [Prakash Mathema/AFP]

Thousands of displaced people are sheltering in aid centres, with little hope of returning home soon. The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors.

Nepali officials say at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, adding that the disaster shows how climate change has hit poor countries that did little to cause it.

title: Climate change made flood-ravaged Nepal vulnerable even before current disaster - The World from PRX
description: Climate change made flood-ravaged Nepal vulnerable even before current disaster  The World from PRX
publisher.title: The World from PRX
full_article:
Local businessman Kedar Prasad Adhikari was standing on the bank of the Trishuli River when he saw the tsunami of destruction barreling toward his home.

Adhikari, 59, remembers the plume of dust that got kicked up as it rushed down the river from the north.

“Initially, it didn’t look like water,” Adhikari said through an interpreter.

The surge of river, mud and rock slammed into the mountainside opposite where he was standing, at a spot where the Trushuli River bends, and whirled into his hometown of Betrawati Bazaar. His wife and son were there.

Terrified for his family, Adhikari watched nearly all 200 buildings in his hometown get knocked down in an instant. He could see that people had rushed to the bridge near his house to take photos of what they thought was a “normal flood.” The bridge — and those people — were swept away.

Massive flash floods sparked by a rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayas struck Nepal and the autonomous Chinese region of Tibet on Aug. 26, leveling towns and leaving more than a thousand people confirmed dead. In a place prone to flooding and already vulnerable to climate change, the destruction was larger than expected. Thousands of people remain missing as recovery efforts continue.

“We never expected this kind of disaster to happen here,” Adhikari said. “It was unexpected, and because of that, so many lives were lost.”

View Image: IMG_0870-Captions3-1024x683.jpg A damaged building in Betrawati in Nepal. Many buildings have been buried multiple stories high in mud and debris after devastating floods. Hannah Chanatry/The World

Adhikari himself was high enough up on the riverbank that he was safe, but that morning, he told The World that he had passed out from fear. And because phone service and electricity went out, it was an agonizing wait before he learned whether his wife and son were safe.

Destabilized by climate change

This region is accustomed to climate-fueled natural disasters.

The Himalayas are warming faster than the rest of the world, and downstream communities are feeling the impact. Thawing permafrost and melting glaciers are causing more landslides, routinely blocking roads, destroying farmland, and stranding residents of mountain villages. Rarely, landslides flatten entire communities.

Glacial lakes, fed by meltwater, are popping up in new places or swelling. When those lakes burst their banks and trigger what scientists call a “glacial lake outburst flood,” the results for downstream communities can be deadly.One hit the Trushuli River valley just last year, killing at least nine people.Locals know this hazard well.

“As the temperatures keep rising, the snow and ice in the mountains begin to melt,” said Govinda Chitrakar, 75, who’s from the devastated riverside town of Devighat.

“When the mountain lakes overflow and landslides carry the water downhill, we end up suffering,” he said, pointing to a mound where a temple and shrine used to be. Until recently, Chitrakar’s hometown was best known as a Hindu holy place.

But what happened late last month was not a glacial lake outburst.

View Image: Screenshot-2026-09-14-at-12.46.45-PM-1024x635.png Rock and mud surged through rivers during the massive flooding sparked by a rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayas recently. Hannah Chanatry/The World

Triggered by ice and rock avalanche

On the morning of Aug. 26, at an elevation of 17,000 feet, a massive chunk of glacier and mountainside broke off the northern side of Langtang Lirungpeak near the border between Tibet and Nepal. It fell some 5,000 feet, where the ice and rock were pulverized. That debris dropped thousands of feet more before slamming into the Trishuli River and creating a slurry of rock, water and sediment that rushed through the narrow mountain valleys at 100 miles an hour.

Nitesh Khadka, a scientist at Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan University, who has studied water and climate risks in the affected area, said it’s not accurate to call what came down the river “floodwater” because there was so much rock and debris in it.

“If it carries something like that, the destructive power of the flood will be high, much more than what we see in typical floods,”Khadka explained. As he walked along the riverbank, he noted the thick layer of sediment the debris slurry deposited on the ground under his feet. It acts like quicksand, one of the many factors confounding rescue and recovery efforts.

The wall of water and rock was initially so high — Khadka estimates roughly 150 feet tall — that it knocked out Nepal’s flood monitoring sensors near the Nepal-Tibet border within a few minutes.

Nepal’s government didn’t even know a flood had been triggered until survivors in the village of Syabrubesicontacted emergency officials to alert them. Only then — roughly half an hour after the flooding started in Nepali territory — did an emergency warning message go out to cell phones in affected areas.

View Image: IMG_5790-Captions2-1024x768.jpg An overturned school bus damaged by massive floods in Betrawati, Nepal. Hannah Chanatry/The World

Baseline conditions

Scientists are still decoding exactly what triggered the tragedy.

Both rock and ice fell from 17,000 feet, but it’s unclear if a bedrock collapse took a glacier down with it or a glacial collapse triggered the piece of mountainside underneath it to break away, too.

“It’s both, but which is more?” asked Kathmandu University glaciologist Mohan Bahadur Chand.

International scientists studying satellite imagery argue it was a bedrock failure that caused the incident. But Chand, who’s studied the glaciers on Langtang Lirungpeak up close in the field, seems to consider the question still open.

He said that after retreating nearly a mile up the mountain in recent years, the glaciers that collapsed were “hanging at the top of a rock cliff” with nothing to support them from below. Warming temperatures also mean it’s raining more at these elevations than it used to, and if rainwater seeped through cracks in the glacier, Chand said that could have acted as a lubricant between the glacier and the bedrock, making the ice above the rock slip.

Like glaciers, the bedrock in the Himalayas is not immune to climate change. As glaciers retreat up mountain slopes, Chand said, more rock is exposed to the elements and the same kind of destructive freeze-thaw cycle that creates potholes in roads.

View Image: Screenshot-2026-09-14-at-1.00.19-PM-1024x659.png Residents in Devighat wait to take a suspension cable car to access the other side of the river, Nepal. Hannah Chanatry/The World

“Of course, the freezing and thawing process that is happening on these elevations, I think these are due to the increasing temperatures,” Chand said. “That could have triggered the collapse.”

Permafrost that has long held these mountain landscapes together is also thawing at higher altitudes, increasing risks in the Himalayas.

To Chand, the link between rising temperatures and what happened to communities in the area is clear — even if the disaster’s cause is still debated.

Other scientists are more cautious, saying more study is needed to pinpoint the cause of the rock-ice collapse before we can understand what fingerprints climate change may have left on the scene.

View Image: Screenshot-2026-09-14-at-12.57.54-PM-1024x648.png A child’s toy car among the debris after devastating floods in Nepal. Hannah Chanatry/The World

‘Nobody expected this’

Everyone agrees, however, that whatever caused the devastation did so in a mountain ecosystem already destabilized by warming temperatures, including people with some of the most intimate knowledge of the area.

Dibas Shrestha, a glaciologist at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, has been monitoring glaciers in Nepal since 2013.

He took his students to the temple town of Devighat to gain a more visceral understanding of what happened.

“Now I realize, I think we neglected glacial hazards,” Shrestha said. “This is a new thing, and I think we should consider this very seriously.”

Nepal’s Foreign Minister, Shisir Khanal, has brought climate change into the conversation very publicly.

View Image: IMG_0857-Captions3-1024x683.jpg People’s personal belongings are scattered on the ground after floods leveled whole towns in Nepal and bordering Tibet. Hannah Chanatry/The World

The week after the disaster, he called on countries that have done the most to fuel warming temperatures by burning fossil fuels to create a fund to help countries like his become more resilient in the face of natural disasters.

“My call to the global community is to not just see this as an unfortunate, one-time incident that occurred in a distant land, but something that human activity, especially climate change caused by human activities, are beginning to have real impact in people’s lives,”Khanal told The World.

That funding is needed not to recover from individual disasters, he said, but to do the work to make future disasters less deadly and destructive.

“If we treat this just as disaster recovery, then we’re not really doing the long-term work that we need to be doing to support our community.”

‘Wouldn’t be able to sleep at night’

More than two weeks after the disaster, 150 people in the town of Betrawati Bazaar are still missing — roughly a fifth of its residents.

After the debris and water retreated, local businessman Kedar Prasad Adhikari eventually learned that his wife and son were safe.

View Image: IMG_0878-Captions3-1024x683.jpg Around 150 people in the town of Betrawati Bazaar remain missing, Nepal. Hannah Chanatry/The World

His son had run up stone steps built into the riverbank to safety. His wife hadn’t been able to run in time, but she caught another break.

“Luckily, the flood came in waves,” Adhikari said, and one of them “pushed my wife quite high on the bank, to the trees, and she grabbed onto one of them.”

The three buildings he used to own, which included his home, hotel, restaurant and a wholesale vegetable business, are now gone. He pointed to the spot where they used to be, which is now just a surging river.

“I won’t rebuild here,” he said through an interpreter. “We’re too scared, we wouldn’t be able to sleep at night.”

title: Bharatiya Temple to Present $100,000 Donation to Sewa International for Nepal Relief and Rehabilitation - newsindiatimes.com
description: Bharatiya Temple to Present $100,000 Donation to Sewa International for Nepal Relief and Rehabilitation  newsindiatimes.com
publisher.title: newsindiatimes.com
full_article:
- ADVERTISEMENT -



On Saturday, September 19, 2026, the Bharatiya Temple which serves Greater Philadelphia region, will present a $100,000 donation to Sewa International, a humanitarian nonprofit organization, in support of relief and rehabilitation efforts for communities affected by the recent disaster in Nepal.

A rescuer helps a woman to move through a muddy road following flash floods and a mudslide in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 28, 2026. REUTERS/Navesh Chitrakar

The presentation ceremony will take place during the Philadelphia Ganesh Festival at Bharatiya Temple.

Event Details



Date: Saturday, September 19, 2026

Check Presentation: 4:00 PM

Venue: Bharatiya Temple

Address: 1612 County Line Road, Montgomeryville, PA 18936

- ADVERTISEMENT -

The funds were raised following a multi-faith prayer gathering held on September 3, 2026, where Hindu, Muslim, Jewish, Sikh, and Christian faith and community leaders came together in prayer, solidarity, and support for the people of Nepal.

The Philadelphia Ganesh Festival, organized by Bharatiya Temple in collaboration with Indian community organizations from throughout the Greater Philadelphia region, is expected to bring together thousands of community members to celebrate Indian religious traditions, culture, music, dance, and community service, the press release said.

This year’s Philadelphia Ganesh Festival is being celebrated from September 14 through September 25, 2026, marking the festival’s 22nd year. September 19 will also feature Outdoor IndiaFest, bringing together religious, cultural, civic, and community leaders for a day of celebration and fellowship.

Over the years, the Greater Philadelphia Hindu community has mobilized support for numerous humanitarian causes, including assistance related to the Kargil conflict, September 11 attacks, Indian Ocean tsunami, Gujarat earthquake, Hurricane Katrina, Nepal earthquake, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

In addition to the Nepal relief check presentation, the September 19 Festival has a number of events planned including:

– Shri Ganesh Maha Abhishekam

– Children’s Ganesh Puja

– Daily Rajopchar Aarti of Lord Ganesha

– Ganrang Dance Competition

– Rajasthani folk music by visiting artists from Rajasthan

– Bharatanatyam recital by Guru Shweta Prachande

– Kathak dance drama by Aditi Bhagwat from Mumbai in support of the Support a Child charity

– Evening Bollywood orchestra by Kalamanch as a tribute to legendary singer Asha Bhosle

The festival program also includes a special Shehnai presentation by Pandit Lokesh Anand for Lord Ganesha.

Website: www. PhiladelphiaGaneshFestival.org

Email: pgfcoreteam@gmail.com

full_article: After her reporting trip to Nepal to cover the devastating floods, Host Carolyn Beeler spoke with Mingma David Sherpa. He’s a world-record-setting mountaineer who has climbed and guided in the Himalayas since 2008. Which means he’s had a front-row view of what warming temperatures are doing to the region.
